ABSTRACT: Physicochemical properties of deep eutectic solvents (DESs) constituted of lithium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (LiTf2N) as the H-bond acceptor (HBA) and three different H-bond donors (HBDs)—urea, acetamide, and 2,2,2-trifluoroaceta-mide—in (1:2), (1:3), and (1:4) mole ratios are investigated. The density of these DESs decreases linearly with increasing temper-ature within the 288–358 K range; it is higher for LiTf2N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide in comparison to LiTf2N/urea and LiTf2N/ acetamide. Density decreases linearly with increasing HBD per mole of LiTf2N. The dynamic viscosity is highest for LiTf2N/urea and lowest for LiTf2N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide; it follows Vogel–Fulcher–Tammann (VFT) temperature dependence. The empirical solvent polarity parameter, E_T^N for all DESs within the investigated temperature range is close to or higher than one, implying these DESs to possess considerably high dipolarity/polarizability and/or HBD acidity. Kamlet–Taft empirical parameters—dipolarity/polarizability (π*), HBD acidity (α), and HBD basicity (β)—reveal that the LiTf₂N/urea DES exhibits the highest π*, followed by LiTf₂N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide and LiTf₂N/acetamide; the α is considerably higher for acetamide DES in comparison. The β values of these DESs are fairly low.

## INTRODUCTION Over the last two decades, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have found their place as potent green alternatives to hazardous organic solvents.1-4 Use of inexpensive and easily available materials has made them a popular choice for synthesis and purification purposes.5,6 Till date, many DESs synthesized mainly from nature-derived substances are in occurrence. The more commonly used are those obtained by mixing quaternary ammonium salts as H-bond acceptors (HBAs) with several H-bond donors (HBDs), such as choline chloride:urea (1:2), choline chloride:glycerol (1:2), and choline chloride:ethylene glycol (1:2).1,2 They have attracted immense popularity owing to their applicability in lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), CO₂ capture, metal extraction, synthesis of pharmaceutical compounds, catalysts in organic synthesis, and many more.4,7-13 However, a relatively less explored family of DESs is the one formed by mixing lithium salts, such as lithium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (LiTf₂N), lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF₆), lithium nitrate (LiNO₃), or lithium chloride (LiCl), with urea- and acetamide-derived compounds.14-17 LiTf₂N-based DESs are particularly more

interesting due to their wide liquid-phase range and the ability of Tf₂N⁻ anion to lower the melting point of the salts. ¹⁸ Recently, a surge in the development and identification of the properties of these DESs has been noticed.

The first liquid binary combination of LiTf2N and urea was reported by Huang et al. in 2001 as a replacement for room- temperature molten salts (RTMS) consisting of alkyl- substituted nitrogen-containing cations, whose synthesis is neither easy nor cost-effective. 19 It is established that the higher affinity of Li⁺ for the oxygen atom of the amide group weakens the interaction between Li⁺ and Tf2N⁻, which further coordinates with the NH₂ group via H-bonding.20 The presence of the CF₃ group in TF₂N⁻ renders the H-bonds even stronger. Le and coworkers have suggested that the formation of DES in the LiTf2N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide mixture is accompanied by the formation of a five-membered ring complex between Li+, the O atom of the CO group, and the F atoms of the CF3 group, since both O and F atoms are negatively charged. 20

The fact that Li-salt-based DESs only contain Li cations is an intriguing characteristic. It is due to this reason, Smiatek et al. noted that, compared to other ionic liquid electrolytes, LiTf₂N and urea-containing DESs may have a greater Li ion transport number.14,21 Electrochemical studies in Li-salt-based DESs have shown promising outcomes. Conventionally used electrolytes in LIBs are mixtures of lithium salts (such as LiPF₆) with ethylene carbonates and ethyl methyl carbonate, which usually degrade and oxidize at higher voltages. In recent times, Li-salt-added choline chloride- based DESs have been gaining popularity in electrochemical applications, but the presence of bulkier choline ions prevents Li ions from transporting to the electrodes. Li-salt-based DESs have an advantage, as they do not contain any other cation. These and many other shortcomings can be overcome by the use of a suitably chosen DES as electrolyte. Li-salt-based DESs offer high thermal stability, ionic conductivity, and nontoxicity, along with cost-effectiveness, a large electrochemical window, and non-flammability.22–25

The Li-salt-based DESs are one step closer in the direction of a novel approach toward environmentally benign solvent systems. Since the discovery of Li-salt-based DESs, their potential to replace other solvent media, such as choline chloride-based DESs and ionic liquids, has not been fully explored; this area remains almost untouched. Only few studies are available describing their utility, majorly in electrochemical applications; however, comprehensive molecular-level insights are still missing. In this work, a detailed physicochemical study of LiTf₂N-based DESs consisting of three different HBDs— urea, acetamide, and 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide—is presented over a wide temperature range. Further knowledge of these DES systems is acquired by changing the mole ratio of LiTf₂N:HBD. To illustrate the dipolarity/polarizability and H-bonding strength among the DES systems, photophysical investigation is carried out using solvatochromic probes. This investigation not only draws some parallels among already existing DESs but also opens new avenues in the field of novel solvents by providing crucial information on their nature and understanding their impact on sustainable development.

Methods. DES of a specific mole ratio was prepared from a precalculated amount of salt, LiTf2N, and the respective HBD using an analytical balance of precision ±0.1 mg, by constant stirring and heating at the same time at about 80 °C for a minimum of 2 h. When a homogeneous mixture was obtained, it was then subjected to vacuum-drying until water was completely ejected. The final water content of DES prior to data acquisition was determined using Karl Fischer titration (KFT) and was found to be less than 100 ppm. Density (p) measurements were carried out using a Mettler Toledo DE45 delta range density meter. Measurements were performed in the temperature range 288–358 K. The standard deviation associated with the density measurement is 0.005 g·cm⁻³. An automated Anton Paar microviscometer (AMVn) with a thermoelectric temperature controller (Peltier-based, with a resolution of 0.01 K and accuracy <0.05 K) was used to study the temperature dependency of dynamic viscosity (η). For improved reproducibility and repeatability of the dynamic viscosity data, the instrument is additionally equipped with various calibrated glass capillaries with sizes of 1.6, 1.8, 3.0, and 4.0 mm. The calculation is based on the classic rolling-ball principle. The deviation in η was estimated to be 2% in the viscosity range spanning between 0.3 and 2500 mPa·s. Electrical conductivity (σ) measurements were carried out on a CM-183 μp-based EC-TDS analyzer with an ATC probe and conductivity cell (CC-03B), purchased from Elico Ltd., India. The standard uncertainty in σ is 2%. The surface tension (γ) was measured at 298 K using a Wilhelmy plate and a DCAT 11EC tensiometer that were obtained from Data-physics. Before each usage, the plate was thoroughly cleaned with Millipore water and rinsed with ethanol to remove any contaminants that might have adhered to it. The plate was heated on a Bunsen burner until it turned hot red and then allowed to cool to room temperature in order to guarantee the total removal of impurities. The standard uncertainty in γ of the solvents is estimated to be 0.05 mN·m⁻¹. The refractive index (nD) was measured by using a digital ABBE refractometer (Labtronics, LT-738) with a standard uncertainty of 0.0002. By comparing the consistency of the observed refractive indices of distilled water and acetone at room temperature (298 K) with the values described in the literature, the ABBE refractometer instrument was calibrated.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION ### Temperature and Composition Dependence of Density. Density of LiTf₂N-containing DESs with three HBDs—acetamide, urea, and 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide—in the LiTf₂N/HBD mole ratios 1:2, 1:3, and 1:4 as a function of temperature in the range 288 to 358 K is experimentally determined and reported in Table 4. Irrespective of the composition and temperature, the density is found to be the highest for DES with 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide as the constituent, followed by urea, and the lowest for acetamide. For mole ratio 1:2 and T = 298 K, densities of LiTf₂N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide, LiTf₂N/urea, and LiTf₂N/acetamide DESs have the values 1.736 g·cm⁻³, 1.676 g·cm⁻³, and 1.540 g·cm⁻³, respectively. It is important to mention here that the density of a DES is primarily controlled by the intermolecular interactions between the constituents,²⁷⁻²⁹ which appear to be the highest in the case of the LiTf₂N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide DES system. Interestingly, the density of 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide (0.960 g·cm⁻³ at 298 K) is lower than that of acetamide (1.16 g·cm⁻³ at 298 K) as well as that of urea (1.32 g·cm⁻³ at 298 K). However, 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide has a much higher molar mass compared to acetamide and urea (113.09 g·mol⁻¹ versus 60.06 and 59.07 g·mol⁻¹, respectively), and due to the presence of highly electronegative fluorine atoms in 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide, the H-bonding and other attractive interactions are the strongest in LiTf₂N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide DESs as opposed to the other two. This renders the relative volume of the LiTf₂N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide DESs to become not as high as expected, thus leading to higher associated densities. Fluorine-containing systems are known to exhibit unusual properties.³⁰,³¹

It is noteworthy that type-III LiTf2N-containing DESs are comparatively denser than type-III choline chloride (ChCl)-based DESs (Table 2).26-35 At ambient conditions, the density of ChCl:HBD (1:2) DESs lies in the range of ~1.1 g·cm⁻³ to ~1.2 g·cm⁻³, which is significantly lower than LiTf2N/HBD DESs. It is usually inferred that the knowledge of the dynamic viscosity of a medium can be related to the strength of intermolecular interactions present among the constituents, which, in the case of DESs, are mainly H-bonding, among others.40,41 In general, the stronger the interactions, the higher the viscous drag. ■ CONCLUSIONS Li-salt-based polar DESs are found to possess widely varying physicochemical properties that depend on the identity of the HBD and the composition. The densities of LiTf2N-containing DESs with urea/acetamide/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide are in between those of ChCl/HBD and lanthanide nitrate hexahydrate salt/urea DESs with similar mole ratios, thus filling the gap in the density of DESs of various types and classes. Dynamic viscosities also vary considerably depending on the identity of the HBD and the composition of these LiTf2N-containing DESs. Electrical conductivity, surface tension, and refractive index of the LiTf2N-based DESs complement those of common solvents, ionic liquids, and other DESs. These Li-salt-based DESs afford appreciable dipolarity/polarizability and H-bond donating acidity, but offer poor H-bond accepting basicity. Electrical conductivity, surface tension, and refractive index of these DESs at 298 K exhibit considerable variation with constituent and composition. The empirical solvent polarity parameter, E_T^N for all DESs within the investigated temperature range is close to or higher than one, implying these DESs to possess considerably high dipolarity/polarizability and/or HBD acidity. Kamlet–Taft empirical parameters—dipolarity/polarizability (π*), HBD acidity (α), and HBD basicity (β)—reveal that the LiTf₂N/urea DES exhibits the highest π*, followed by LiTf₂N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide and LiTf₂N/acetamide; the α is considerably higher for acetamide DES in comparison. The β values of these DESs are fairly low. ## INTRODUCTION Over the last two decades, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have found their place as potent green alternatives to hazardous organic solvents.1-4 Use of inexpensive and easily available materials has made them a popular choice for synthesis and purification purposes.5,6 Till date, many DESs synthesized mainly from nature-derived substances are in occurrence. The more commonly used are those obtained by mixing quaternary ammonium salts as H-bond acceptors (HBAs) with several H-bond donors (HBDs), such as choline chloride:urea (1:2), choline chloride:glycerol (1:2), and choline chloride:ethylene glycol (1:2).1,2 They have attracted immense popularity owing to their applicability in lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), CO₂ capture, metal extraction, synthesis of pharmaceutical compounds, catalysts in organic synthesis, and many more.4,7-13 However, a relatively less explored family of DESs is the one formed by mixing lithium salts, such as lithium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (LiTf₂N), lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF₆), lithium nitrate (LiNO₃), or lithium chloride (LiCl), with urea- and acetamide-derived compounds.14-17 LiTf₂N-based DESs are particularly more interesting due to their wide liquid-phase range and the ability of Tf₂N⁻ anion to lower the melting point of the salts. ¹⁸ Recently, a surge in the development and identification of the properties of these DESs has been noticed. The first liquid binary combination of LiTf2N and urea was reported by Huang et al. in 2001 as a replacement for room- temperature molten salts (RTMS) consisting of alkyl- substituted nitrogen-containing cations, whose synthesis is neither easy nor cost-effective. 19 It is established that the higher affinity of Li⁺ for the oxygen atom of the amide group weakens the interaction between Li⁺ and Tf2N⁻, which further coordinates with the NH₂ group via H-bonding.20 The presence of the CF₃ group in TF₂N⁻ renders the H-bonds even stronger. Le and coworkers have suggested that the formation of DES in the LiTf2N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide mixture is accompanied by the formation of a five-membered ring complex between Li+, the O atom of the CO group, and the F atoms of the CF3 group, since both O and F atoms are negatively charged. 20 The fact that Li-salt-based DESs only contain Li cations is an intriguing characteristic. It is due to this reason, Smiatek et al. noted that, compared to other ionic liquid electrolytes, LiTf₂N and urea-containing DESs may have a greater Li ion transport number.14,21 Electrochemical studies in Li-salt-based DESs have shown promising outcomes. Conventionally used electrolytes in LIBs are mixtures of lithium salts (such as LiPF₆) with ethylene carbonates and ethyl methyl carbonate, which usually degrade and oxidize at higher voltages. In recent times, Li-salt-added choline chloride- based DESs have been gaining popularity in electrochemical applications, but the presence of bulkier choline ions prevents Li ions from transporting to the electrodes. Li-salt-based DESs have an advantage, as they do not contain any other cation. These and many other shortcomings can be overcome by the use of a suitably chosen DES as electrolyte. Li-salt-based DESs offer high thermal stability, ionic conductivity, and nontoxicity, along with cost-effectiveness, a large electrochemical window, and non-flammability.22–25 The Li-salt-based DESs are one step closer in the direction of a novel approach toward environmentally benign solvent systems. Since the discovery of Li-salt-based DESs, their potential to replace other solvent media, such as choline chloride-based DESs and ionic liquids, has not been fully explored; this area remains almost untouched. Only few studies are available describing their utility, majorly in electrochemical applications; however, comprehensive molecular-level insights are still missing. In this work, a detailed physicochemical study of LiTf₂N-based DESs consisting of three different HBDs— urea, acetamide, and 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide—is presented over a wide temperature range. Further knowledge of these DES systems is acquired by changing the mole ratio of LiTf₂N:HBD. To illustrate the dipolarity/polarizability and H-bonding strength among the DES systems, photophysical investigation is carried out using solvatochromic probes. This investigation not only draws some parallels among already existing DESs but also opens new avenues in the field of novel solvents by providing crucial information on their nature and understanding their impact on sustainable development. ## EXPERIMENTAL METHODS **Materials.** All DES constituents, including LiTf₂N, acetamide, urea, and 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide, were acquired from Sigma-Aldrich and used without further purification. Density of LiTf₂N-containing DESs with three HBDs—acetamide, urea, and 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide—in the LiTf₂N/HBD mole ratios 1:2, 1:3, and 1:4 as a function of temperature in the range 288 to 358 K is experimentally determined and reported in Table 4. Irrespective of the composition and temperature, the density is found to be the highest for DES with 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide as the constituent, followed by urea, and the lowest for acetamide. For mole ratio 1:2 and T = 298 K, densities of LiTf₂N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide, LiTf₂N/urea, and LiTf₂N/acetamide DESs have the values 1.736 g·cm⁻³, 1.676 g·cm⁻³, and 1.540 g·cm⁻³, respectively. It is important to mention here that the density of a DES is primarily controlled by the intermolecular interactions between the constituents,²⁷⁻²⁹ which appear to be the highest in the case of the LiTf₂N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide DES system. Interestingly, the density of 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide (0.960 g·cm⁻³ at 298 K) is lower than that of acetamide (1.16 g·cm⁻³ at 298 K) as well as that of urea (1.32 g·cm⁻³ at 298 K). This renders the relative volume of the LiTf₂N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide DESs to become not as high as expected, thus leading to higher associated densities. The more commonly used are those obtained by mixing quaternary ammonium salts as H-bond acceptors (HBAs) with several H-bond donors (HBDs), such as choline chloride:urea (1:2), choline chloride:glycerol (1:2), and choline chloride:ethylene glycol (1:2).1,2 They have attracted immense popularity owing to their applicability in lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), CO₂ capture, metal extraction, synthesis of pharmaceutical compounds, catalysts in organic synthesis, and many more.4,7-13 However, a relatively less explored family of DESs is the one formed by mixing lithium salts, such as lithium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (LiTf₂N), lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF₆), lithium nitrate (LiNO₃), or lithium chloride (LiCl), with urea- and acetamide-derived compounds.14-17 LiTf₂N-based DESs are particularly more interesting due to their wide liquid-phase range and the ability of Tf₂N⁻ anion to lower the melting point of the salts. ¹⁸ Recently, a surge in the development and identification of the properties of these DESs has been noticed. The first liquid binary combination of LiTf2N and urea was reported by Huang et al. in 2001 as a replacement for room- temperature molten salts (RTMS) consisting of alkyl- substituted nitrogen-containing cations, whose synthesis is neither easy nor cost-effective. 19 It is established that the higher affinity of Li⁺ for the oxygen atom of the amide group weakens the interaction between Li⁺ and Tf2N⁻, which further coordinates with the NH₂ group via H-bonding.20 The presence of the CF₃ group in TF₂N⁻ renders the H-bonds even stronger. Density of LiTf₂N-containing DESs with three HBDs—acetamide, urea, and 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide—in the LiTf₂N/HBD mole ratios 1:2, 1:3, and 1:4 as a function of temperature in the range 288 to 358 K is experimentally determined and reported in Table 4. For mole ratio 1:2 and T = 298 K, densities of LiTf₂N/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide, LiTf₂N/urea, and LiTf₂N/acetamide DESs have the values 1.736 g·cm⁻³, 1.676 g·cm⁻³, and 1.540 g·cm⁻³, respectively. The combination of higher π* and lower α and vice versa results in similar E_T^N values of the investigated DES systems as ~68% of the contribution to E_T^N is from the HBD acidity of the milieu.⁵⁶,⁵⁷ In comparison, DESs formed by mixing urea with hydrated lanthanide salts have been reported to exhibit exceptionally high π*; a π* of 1.70 is exhibited by gadolinium salt (Gd)-containing DES (Gd: urea in a 1:2 molar ratio). The π* ranged from 1.50 to 1.70 for the lanthanide salts-urea DESs. 58 In this context, the LiTf2N- containing DES systems can also be considered to exhibit significantly high dipolarity/polarizability. In comparison, for choline chloride (ChCl)-based DESs, the reported π* is only 1.23 for (ChCl:urea:: 1:2), 59 1.373 for (ChCl:citric acid:: 1:1),68 and 1.406 for (ChCl:ZnCl2:: 1:2).68 The highest π* for any DES that is reported earlier was 1.671 for (betaine:citric acid:1:1)68 under ambient conditions. The vis-à-vis absorption maxima of both DENA and NA, respectively, show a decrease upon increasing temperature (Figures S2 and S3). While not much variation is observed in HBA basicity of DESs with change in temperature, as expected, the dipolarity/polarizability does decrease monotonically with increasing temperature. The increased average thermal reorientation of the dipoles leads to the destruction of the cooperative effect, resulting in decreased dielectric constant with increasing temperature. While the LiTf₂N-containing DESs investigated in this work offer considerably high HBD acidity (α), especially by LiTf₂N/acetamide DES (vide supra), the HBA basicity (β) of these DES systems is fairly low (ranging from 0.06 to 0.14 only, with no apparent trend). This, combined with the estimated Eᵀ values, shows widely varying physicochemical properties offered by the LiTf₂N-containig DES systems investigated here. ■ CONCLUSIONS Li-salt-based polar DESs are found to possess widely varying physicochemical properties that depend on the identity of the HBD and the composition. The densities of LiTf2N-containing DESs with urea/acetamide/2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide are in between those of ChCl/HBD and lanthanide nitrate hexahydrate salt/urea DESs with similar mole ratios, thus filling the gap in the density of DESs of various types and classes. Dynamic viscosities also vary considerably depending on the identity of the HBD and the composition of these LiTf2N-containing DESs. Electrical conductivity, surface tension, and refractive index of the LiTf2N-based DESs complement those of common solvents, ionic liquids, and other DESs. These Li-salt-based DESs afford appreciable dipolarity/polarizability and H-bond donating acidity, but offer poor H-bond accepting basicity.
